xhosa-kingdom.t: The united Xhosa paramountcy of the Tshawe royal house, which expanded westward to meet the Cape Colony's frontier before splitting in two.
xhosa-kingdom.o: The Xhosa were the south-westernmost Nguni-speaking people, and their royal Tshawe lineage traditionally asserted supremacy over other clans in the region between the Mbashe and Kei rivers. By the 17th century the Xhosa paramount was recognised by a growing confederation of chiefdoms, many incorporating Khoikhoi groups.
xhosa-kingdom.r: The paramount ruled through royal kin who governed their own chiefdoms with considerable independence, advised by councils of counsellors. Wealth was measured in cattle, and expansion came through younger sons founding new chiefdoms in fresh pastures. Under Tshiwo and Phalo the Xhosa moved west towards the Fish River, absorbing Khoikhoi and gaining clicks in their language.
xhosa-kingdom.e: A dispute between Phalo's sons Gcaleka and Rharhabe split the paramountcy, and on Phalo's death around 1775 it divided into the Gcaleka Xhosa Kingdom east of the Kei and the Rharhabe Xhosa Kingdom to the west, just as frontier wars with the Cape Colony began.

xianbei.t: The nomadic confederation that replaced the Xiongnu on the Mongolian steppe, whose clans later founded the Northern Wei and other dynasties of northern China.
xianbei.o: The Xianbei were descendants of the Donghu who fled to the Xianbei mountains in the north-east after the Xiongnu destroyed them around 206 BCE. For two centuries they lived under Xiongnu domination in eastern Inner Mongolia and Manchuria. When Han armies broke the Northern Xiongnu in 87 to 91 CE, the Xianbei moved west and absorbed tens of thousands of Xiongnu households.
xianbei.r: Around 156 CE the chieftain Tanshihuai united the tribes into a confederation stretching from Manchuria to the Tarim, divided into eastern, central and western sections, and raided the Han Dynasty frontier almost yearly. They lived as mounted herders and spoke an early Mongolic language. Power depended on the prestige of individual leaders rather than a fixed dynasty.
xianbei.e: Tanshihuai's confederation broke up after his death around 181. The chieftain Kebineng rebuilt a large federation until Cao Wei agents assassinated him in 235. Xianbei clans such as the Murong, Tuoba, Duan Xianbei and Yuwen Xianbei went on to found states including the Northern Wei.

xia-dou-jiande.t: The rebel kingdom of Dou Jiande on the Hebei plain, remembered as the most humane of the Sui-era insurgent regimes, destroyed at the Battle of Hulao in 621.
xia-dou-jiande.o: Dou Jiande, a village headman from Zhangnan in Hebei, joined the peasant risings against Emperor Yang's levies for the Goguryeo wars in 611. He took over the band of Gao Shida, proclaimed himself Prince of Changle in 617 and Prince of Xia in 618, ruling much of Hebei from Lezhou.
xia-dou-jiande.r: Dou Jiande won a reputation for frugality, for sparing captured Sui officials and employing them in his government, and for sharing spoils with his soldiers. In 619 he defeated and executed Yuwen Huaji, the murderer of Emperor Yang, which raised his standing among loyalists of the Sui Dynasty.
xia-dou-jiande.e: In 621 he marched to relieve Wang Shichong, besieged at Luoyang by the Tang. Li Shimin blocked him at the Hulao pass and captured him; he was executed at Chang'an. His former officers under Liu Heita rose again and held out until 623.

xia-dynasty.t: China's traditional first dynasty, founded by the flood-taming Yu the Great; whether it was a real state remains one of the great open questions of Chinese archaeology.
xia-dynasty.o: Later histories, above all Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, describe the Xia as the dynasty founded when Yu the Great, rewarded for controlling the floods of the Yellow River, passed power to his son Qi, making rule hereditary. The register follows the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project's dates. No writing survives from the period itself.
xia-dynasty.r: Everything known comes from texts written a thousand years later or from archaeology. Many scholars link the Xia with the Erlitou culture of the Luoyang basin in Henan, which built palace compounds on rammed-earth platforms, cast the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels and made jade blades. Whether Erlitou was the Xia, and what its people called themselves, cannot be proved without inscriptions.
xia-dynasty.e: Tradition holds that the last king, Jie, was a tyrant overthrown by Tang, founder of the Shang dynasty, at the Battle of Mingtiao. The Xia became the model of the first legitimate dynasty, and later Chinese political thought used its fall as the classic example of Heaven withdrawing its favour from a corrupt ruler.

xueyantuo.t: A Tiele tribe that briefly ruled the Mongolian steppe after the fall of the Eastern Turks, before Tang China destroyed it in 646.
xueyantuo.o: The Xueyantuo were one of the Tiele tribes of the steppe, subject to the Turkic khagans. In 628 they rebelled against the Eastern Turkic Khaganate under their leader Yinan, who was recognised by Tang Taizong as Zhenzhu Khagan. After the Turks fell in 630 they became the dominant power in Mongolia.
xueyantuo.r: Zhenzhu Khagan ruled a confederation of Tiele tribes including the Uyghurs, and could reportedly field 200,000 horsemen. He balanced between alliance and rivalry with the Tang, negotiating a marriage alliance that Taizong ultimately cancelled, and clashed with Turks resettled by the Tang south of the Gobi.
xueyantuo.e: After Zhenzhu Khagan's death in 645, his son Duomi Khagan attacked Tang territory. In 646 a Tang army, aided by the Uyghurs and other Tiele tribes, destroyed the Xueyantuo. Their lands came under Tang protectorates, and the Uyghurs later rose to dominate the same region.
